articles.title: Today in Supreme Court History: November 22, 1963
articles.content:
11/22/1963: President Lyndon B. Johnson takes the oath of office. He would appoint two Justices to the Supreme Court: Abe Fortas and Thurgood Marshall.

articles.title: America Needs More Nurses. The Trump Administration Wants To Make Them Much Harder To Hire.
articles.content:
The Trump administration is seeking to make it more difficult for employers to sponsor workers for green cards, offering sweeping potential changes to the federal program that governs the steps people must take to hire foreign employees for permanent residence in the United States.
Its plan covers a lot of ground. The most seismic change, though, is arguably the elimination of a rule that allows employers to circumvent the time-consuming labor market test when hiring nurses and physical therapists, two crucial occupations the government has long recognized as suffering from labor shortages.
The full proposal, recently published by the Department of Labor, would broadly alter the permanent labor certification (PERM) program in a few significant ways. Employers would be prohibited from filing a PERM application within two years of laying off U.S. workers in "the same or similar occupation." (Current law mandates six months.) If such a layoff occurs after a PERM application has been filed, employers would be obligated to consider laid-off U.S. workers over "a significantly broader timeframe"—one extending through the adjudication of an immigrant's petition. It would also mandate longer recruiting periods and an expanded approach to job advertising.
The PERM program already presents significant bureaucratic hurdles to employers—as it stands, its rules are meant to ensure that "no able, qualified, and available U.S. workers who are willing to accept the permanent job offer" and that hiring someone from abroad "will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers." The process, as a result, is strict and cumbersome.
Schedule A, the exemption, thus allows employers to bypass the standard process when hiring for certain vital roles experiencing nationwide shortages. "We have determined there are not sufficient United States workers who are able, willing, qualified, and available for the occupations listed below on Schedule A and the wages and working conditions of United States workers similarly employed will not be adversely affected by the employment of aliens in Schedule A occupations," the regulation reads. The intent was to make a burdensome law more nimble and responsive.
So why the change? "The Department likewise cannot justify continuing to waive recruitment for U.S. workers as it no longer possesses evidence that there is a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers able, willing, qualified, and available to work as physical therapists or professional nurses," the proposal says, "as required for their placement on Schedule A."
The data do not appear to support that contention. "There is a projected 8% shortage of registered nurses (RNs) in 2028. By 2038, the shortage is 3%," which amounts to a shortage of 108,960 full-time nurses, the National Center for Health Workforce Analysis noted in a recent report. Notably, "these projections assume that historical patterns of attrition, graduation, and labor force participation remain the same over the forecast period." The American Physical Therapy Association, meanwhile, forecasted a 3.3 percent shortfall for 2037.
In practice, the proposed change—which is open for comment through January 19—would require healthcare employers to run a red-tape-ridden bureaucratic gauntlet to fill critical medical roles. "Run" may not be the appropriate word when considering how much waiting is involved—a mix of exertion and atrophy. It's plausible, in other words, that this would exacerbate an existing labor shortage in an industry where time is in short supply. Is that worth the tradeoff?

articles.title: Rents, Internet Speeds, and Airfares: 3 Deregulation Success Stories From Milei's Argentina
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
Argentina's deregulatory push may be the most significant story yet to come out of Javier Milei's presidency. After launching the Ministry of Deregulation and State Transformation and putting economist Federico Sturzenegger in charge of it, the Milei administration has been butting heads with crony capitalists, entrenched unions, and other beneficiaries of decades of corporatist policies. The results have not just been a boon for Argentina. As cronyism gets stronger in the United States and overregulation paralyzes Europe's economy, Milei is offering an example to the rest of the world.
"Freeze the rent" was one of Zohran Mamdani's core proposals as he ran for mayor of New York on what was pitched as an affordability platform. Now that he's in office, rents have indeed been frozen on approximately 1 million apartments.
Affordability was also a major concern when Milei took office in December 2023, but Argentina has taken the opposite course. Its leaders understand that state action had caused unaffordable housing.
The country's 2020 rental law required rental contracts to run at least three years, capped annual rent increases to a central bank–calculated blend of inflation and wage growth, mandated payment in pesos only, and made early termination by landlords virtually impossible. As a result, rents grew 1.7 times the pace of inflation the year the law passed and a further 50 percent in 2023.
In a context of rising inflation (up from 36 percent in 2020 to 211 percent in 2023), the law made it almost impossible for landlords to earn or even calculate a profit—unless they set an extraordinarily high initial price to cover expected inflation. That ultimately drove rents higher. Panic ensued, with long-term rental listings plunging by 53 percent over the course of three years. Landlords were fleeing to Airbnb, making informal agreements with people they knew personally, putting up their property for sale, or simply leaving spaces vacant.
Renters, in turn, were faced with impossible scenarios. Palermo, a Buenos Aires district of 250,000 people, at one point had only about a dozen listings on Zonaprop, one of the country's largest real estate platforms. People signed up for alerts and sought to secure a lease immediately after seeing a new listing. With fierce competition for the small number of available apartments, many took their chances with "temporary," short-term arrangements that mimicked regular leases but were in fact illegal. The unlucky ones just couldn't move.
On December 20, 2023, just 10 days after taking office, Milei signed DNU 70/23, an executive order that repealed the 2020 rental control and replaced it with nothing. The results were immediate: By June 2024, the rental housing supply in the Buenos Aires metropolitan area was 212 percent higher. Over the same time period, real rent prices went down almost 27 percent.
More than two and a half years after rent control's repeal, the housing rental market has essentially kept those initial gains. According to an index published by the real estate agent Soledad Balayan, supply in the city of Buenos Aires has been stable during 2026. Moreover, according to Zonaprop, the average rent for a one-bedroom apartment has pretty much tracked the inflation rate since 2025, indicating that the market has finally stabilized.
Now Sturzenegger hopes to drive prices further down by strengthening property rights and deregulating the real estate market. To that end, a bill on the "inviolability of private property" was passed by the Senate in August and is now under discussion in the House. Among other measures, the proposed law would facilitate evictions for nonpayment, squatting, or land seizures. Right now, there is a lot of legal uncertainty around those areas. Evicting a renter over nonpayment, for example, requires a judge's order following a lengthy trial, which can drag on for up to 18 months. That process deters many potential landlords from entering the market.
Sturzenegger is also pushing an amendment that would eliminate mandatory licensing for real estate brokers and minimum commission rates, thus addressing the problem of high brokerage fees. A 2024 study by the consulting firm Miglino y Asociados found that Argentina's average fee of 6 percent is among the highest in the world.
The story of how satellite internet developed in Argentina follows a similar script. Once again, the Milei administration made a clean break: It got the state out of the way.
In fact, satellite internet deregulation happened on the same day as the end of rent control. DNU 70/23 was called a megadecreto, or megadecree, because it issued a number of directives across Argentina's regulatory environment. Besides repealing rent control, it removed a complex system of authorizations to provide satellite internet services, then effectively monopolized by a state-owned company called ARSAT. Starlink, the world's largest satellite internet company, had been making a long and laborious attempt to enter the market; though it had been granted a provisional authorization in 2021, it was still not allowed to operate in Argentina.
Resistance to opening up the satellite internet market was not just coming from Arsat, though. Sturzenegger has suggested that Grupo Clarín—Argentina's largest media conglomerate and also an internet provider—influenced the regulatory agency. Smaller internet providers in the countryside also benefited from the status quo, charging high prices for low-quality services.
No satellite internet meant, for many, barely any internet connection at all. By the time Milei became president, in Buenos Aires, where there were multiple providers and it made sense to invest in fiber-optic cable, it was possible to get a 100 Mbps connection for about $8 per month. Not so in the sparsely populated countryside. In 2023, Pedro Gassiebayle, a livestock farmer in the northern province of Corrientes, paid about $30 a month for 10 Mbps service on his farm. That would have been considered high-quality elsewhere in 2013.
Besides being slow and expensive, internet services were limited and unreliable. Since Gassiebayle's internet connection came from a small town near his farm, he says, "whenever there was wind or rain, the power in town would always go out, so we'd lose both power and internet." He adds: "Sometimes they'd even cut power preventively to avoid electrical risk." Moreover, coverage was only available at the farmhouse, since Gassiebayle's provider—the only one available in the area—could not get to his farm's outposts. His employees had to climb the roof at their outposts to try to get a signal to communicate with him or among each other. When there was trouble—if, say, a fire broke out—critical time was lost.
Three years later, Gassiebayle is a happy customer of Starlink. For the same $30 as before, he now gets up to 250 Mbps of speed. Satellite internet also means the connection no longer comes from a nearby town—and since he has a battery ready for a power outage, he can have internet access for hours even without power. The farm's employees can now communicate with ease, as Starlink can service all of the farm outposts. Gassiebayle spends more time on his farm instead of leaving for the city because he can still be connected with the rest of the world.
But this is bigger than farming. The communications revolution in Argentina's interior is playing a key part in the country's economy. As of July, the official data show both that agricultural activity is up 28 percent from July 2023 and that mining activity is also up 30 percent, fueled by tax reductions, lower tariffs, and fewer regulations—mostly as part of a Milei-championed incentive scheme known as RIGI—that continue to attract new investment.
Like farming, mining and energy operations take place in remote areas that have virtually no fiber-optic infrastructure and have benefited from the arrival of satellite internet. Take the Vaca Muerta oil formation, which extends across the western provinces of Neuquén, Mendoza, and Río Negro and has become Argentina's main source of oil. In Vaca Muerta, companies that previously relied on bad internet have now improved operations. Luis Aiassa—the CEO of Rakiduamn, a Río Negro–based operation that provides technological support in the region—last year called connectivity the company's "main obstacle." Now that Starlink has teamed up with the local business Movistar to service corporate customers in the area, that is no longer the case.
How has satellite internet changed life in Argentina's interior? In a recent paper, Deregulation: From Theory to Practice, Sturzenegger describes a lodge owner in Patagonia who told him he now gets more guests, as tourists know they can work remotely from there. In April, a video went viral showing a mule carrying a Starlink Mini antenna so that horse riders in a historic high-mountain crossing event in San Juan could stay in touch with organizers. Even now, mentions of Starlink on Argentine social media still draw thousands of comments by people who remember how difficult and expensive it was to get service outside of cities.
At zero cost to the state, satellite internet is now available for virtually any Argentine who needs it. The space is shaping up to be a competitive one: While Elon Musk's company currently dominates, a competitor called Myriota has also recently started operations, and Amazon Leo is expected to launch a service soon too.
Starting in 1971, the state-owned Aerolíneas Argentinas was guaranteed a share of at least 50 percent of the entire aviation market. Then the megadecreto eliminated that mandate.
In 2024, another decree opened up the ground-handling business, which had been monopolized by the state-owned Intercargo since 1990. The same decree let airlines set ticket prices freely, and it allowed any airline to sell tickets to the state, a privilege that only Aerolíneas Argentinas enjoyed until then. It also eliminated a requirement that each new route be approved by the president himself instead of the regulatory agency. Other red tape was cut as well: Nationality requirements for crews were dropped, for example.
For Aerolíneas Argentinas and Intercargo, deregulation and a focus on efficiency have started to reverse the lousy reputations the companies had earned. Both had lost money in the pre-Milei era—particularly Aerolíneas Argentinas, which lost an average of $500 million a year from 2008, the year it was renationalized, through 2023. In 2025, by contrast, the company posted a surplus for the first time since nationalization.
Thanks to deregulation and a more stable exchange rate, domestic airfares across Argentina dropped 14 percent in 2025 compared to 2024, according to a study by the consulting firm Fundación Ecosur. Adjusted for inflation, the drop was 42 percent. On popular routes where competition had previously been restricted, price drops have been dramatic: A flight between Buenos Aires and Córdoba (Argentina's second-largest city by population) cost 67 percent less in real terms in 2025 relative to 2024.
Smaller markets across the country are also benefiting from liberalization. For example, a new commuter airline called Humming Airways now flies from Buenos Aires to such cities as Paraná (population 270,000), Concordia (180,000), and Olavarría (125,000) with aircraft that carry up to 19 passengers. These new flights are usually more expensive than traveling by bus, but they save customers a lot of time.
Candela Echezarreta, a resident doctor at Hospital Italiano in Buenos Aires, is one of Humming Airways' new customers, having flown twice already between that city and her hometown of Concordia. The trip, which normally takes over four hours by car or more than six by bus, takes less than an hour by air. "That simplifies everything," she says. The flights are on time, and the check-in process in Concordia is quick. She wishes there were more flights so they wouldn't all fall in the middle of the week, but overall, she says, "it's a great alternative."
Concordia's airport has now been renovated and looks like new—and it's not the only one, since deregulation measures have allowed other airports to reopen. The airfield in Chos Malal (population 15,000) was closed before Milei took over, but it restarted operations in September.
While it is not easy to calibrate air traffic demand for smaller cities, the provisional results seem positive. Because it relies on small aircraft, Humming Airways' average load factor stood at 75 percent in 2025. The new airline adds and drops destinations as it discovers which are profitable. Some flights, in turn, have been reclassified as seasonal, and others have recently been temporarily interrupted after a bird strike put an aircraft out of service. But the airline has since bought two new planes to add backup capacity, a sign it is expanding rather than pulling back.
So what's next for aviation markets in Argentina? Milei wants to privatize state-owned companies, but that has moved slowly because of the political context. Aerolíneas Argentinas is still owned by the state because Congress refused to include it in a list of permitted privatizations. An attempt to sell Intercargo stalled after the government sought to auction it off, but no bids were placed; experts paradoxically cited the lack of future monopoly privileges as one of the reasons for the lack of buyers. (Four other companies now compete in the ground-handling business.) The Milei administration is now considering breaking up the company to make it more attractive to investors.
In any case, there is still politically sensitive work to be done on regulations, particularly as they relate to labor relations with pilots. The administration's efforts to update pilot flight-time and rest rules were stopped when a labor court suspended the decree under which rules were changed. While a final ruling is pending, pilots are only allowed to fly a maximum of 800 hours a year, compared to Europe's 900 or 1,000 in the U.S. (the latter being the limit pursued by the Milei administration).
Those are just some of the deregulatory measures that the Milei administration has taken. During his first year, he deregulated something every day. As of mid-August, the Ministry of Deregulation reports, the government has modified or eliminated more than 2,800 regulations, spanning everything from cooking-gas pricing to customs procedures for small exporters.
Deregulation is contentious. In some cases, the administration has had to negotiate with interest groups that fiercely cling to the legal privileges they enjoy. In July, for example, the government issued a decree that would have allowed the free negotiation of harbor pilot fees and eased entry requirements for new pilots, with the goal of driving down prices. (Exporters and importers pay four times more in Argentina than in the U.S. for the same pilotage services.) But the harbor pilots went on strike, nearly paralyzing trade for a few days. In the end, they agreed to a 20 percent cut in fees but forced the government to reinstate the old regulation in return.
Whenever Milei has managed to implement far-reaching deregulation, the results have been impressive. Repealing rent control tripled supply and drove rent down by 27 percent in a matter of months. Eliminating price floors for flights made domestic airfares plunge by 42 percent in just a year. Opening up the satellite internet market induced a 25-fold improvement in speed in the countryside. For almost three years, Argentina has been lighting a deregulatory path for the world.
The post Rents, Internet Speeds, and Airfares: 3 Deregulation Success Stories From Milei's Argentina appeared first on Reason Magazine.

Because it relies on small aircraft, Humming Airways' average load factor stood at 75 percent in 2025. The new airline adds and drops destinations as it discovers which are profitable. Some flights, in turn, have been reclassified as seasonal, and others have recently been temporarily interrupted after a bird strike put an aircraft out of service. But the airline has since bought two new planes to add backup capacity, a sign it is expanding rather than pulling back.

So what's next for aviation markets in Argentina? Milei wants to privatize state-owned companies, but that has moved slowly because of the political context. Aerolíneas Argentinas is still owned by the state because Congress refused to include it in a list of permitted privatizations. An attempt to sell Intercargo stalled after the government sought to auction it off, but no bids were placed; experts paradoxically cited the lack of future monopoly privileges as one of the reasons for the lack of buyers. (Four other companies now compete in the ground-handling business.) The Milei administration is now considering breaking up the company to make it more attractive to investors.

In any case, there is still politically sensitive work to be done on regulations, particularly as they relate to labor relations with pilots. The administration's efforts to update pilot flight-time and rest rules were stopped when a labor court suspended the decree under which rules were changed. While a final ruling is pending, pilots are only allowed to fly a maximum of 800 hours a year, compared to Europe's 900 or 1,000 in the U.S. (the latter being the limit pursued by the Milei administration).

Learning the Lessons

Those are just some of the deregulatory measures that the Milei administration has taken. During his first year, he deregulated something every day. As of mid-August, the Ministry of Deregulation reports, the government has modified or eliminated more than 2,800 regulations, spanning everything from cooking-gas pricing to customs procedures for small exporters.

Deregulation is contentious. In some cases, the administration has had to negotiate with interest groups that fiercely cling to the legal privileges they enjoy. In July, for example, the government issued a decree that would have allowed the free negotiation of harbor pilot fees and eased entry requirements for new pilots, with the goal of driving down prices. (Exporters and importers pay four times more in Argentina than in the U.S. for the same pilotage services.) But the harbor pilots went on strike, nearly paralyzing trade for a few days. In the end, they agreed to a 20 percent cut in fees but forced the government to reinstate the old regulation in return.

Whenever Milei has managed to implement far-reaching deregulation, the results have been impressive. Repealing rent control tripled supply and drove rent down by 27 percent in a matter of months. Eliminating price floors for flights made domestic airfares plunge by 42 percent in just a year. Opening up the satellite internet market induced a 25-fold improvement in speed in the countryside. For almost three years, Argentina has been lighting a deregulatory path for the world.

articles.title: The Quorum Clause Case
articles.content:
In 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy. At the time, there were ample warnings that this process had constitutional infirmities, but the House pressed ahead. Indeed, the House of Representatives continued to use the proxy rule through the end of 2022. One such bill was the Consolidation Appropriations Act of 2023. At this time, the justification for social distancing had passed. The new House assembled in January 2023. I see no masks. Members of Congress are walking around with their families.
At the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled. Look at this picture. I don't see many members wearing masks.
Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.
The pandemic was only a few years ago, but it is important to remember how many brazen violations of the Constitution there were in short order. As Justice Gorsuch wrote in Roman Catholic Diocese v. Brooklyn v. Cuomo, "Even if the Constitution has taken a holiday during this pandemic, it cannot become a sabbatical." The proxy rule was one such sabbatical.
In 2023, Texas challenged the constitutionality of one provision of the appropriations bill, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. In 2024, Judge Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas wrote a magisterial opinion that stretched more than one-hundred pages. He explained in depth why the enrolled bill doctrine does not block review and why the proxy rule violates the quorum clause. At the time, I read the opinion and thought Judge Hendrix put forward an extremely justification. The House tried to take a shortcut and got caught. A panel of the Fifth Circuit reversed, but now the en banc Fifth Circuit has affirmed Judge Hendrix's decision.
I'll admit, the immediate reaction to this decision is "it can't be right!" This intuition, I submit, is based more on the consequences than the merits. If every bill passed during the COVID period is now subject to a constitutional challenge, the consequences could be serious. But I encourage you to back off the consequentialism. Far too many judges and lawyers start with the consequences and work their way backwards. If the House of Representatives decided to take a shortcut and ignored a constitutional requirement, then the members of that body should bear the consequences of their decision.
The en banc Fifth Circuit split (as if often does) by a 9-8 vote. Thankfully, there were no senior judges on the three-judge panel. Judge Wilson wrote the majority opinion and Judge Graves wrote the dissent. Judge Haynes continues her unusual practice where she doesn't join any opinion, reducing her thoughts to a single footnote.
* Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.
Judge Haynes might think she is being clever, but I doubt anyone else agrees. Indeed, in a number of recent cases, Judge Haynes simply writes that she affirms for the reasons stated by the district court--as if nothing that her colleagues wrote made a difference. I think it shows a lack of respect to her colleagues who spend considerable time preparing opinions and she doesn't even bother explaining where she disagrees. She is capable of writing reasoned opinions, but just shrugs at the en banc stage.
Judges Wilson and Judge Graves agree that Texas has standing. They further agree that the enrolled bill rule does not preclude review. The disagreement is purely a legal question about whether the proxy rule violates the Quorum Clause. Having read both the majority and dissenting opinions, I don't think the issue is even close. The strongest argument for the dissent is the "Unanimous Consent" rule, and the majority demolishes that argument.
What happens next? It's complicated.
I am fairly certain that the new Attorney General opposes this case and will do everything in his power to scuttle the suit, as well as the Fifth Circuit's en banc precedent. In recent days, the Texas Attorney General has been dismissing and settling many cases. The reason, I suspect, is to avoid giving the new Attorney General a vehicle to enter into binding consent decrees. I suppose it is conceivable that Texas will try to enter into some kind of settlement with the United States. Or maybe Texas just moves to dismiss the case with prejudice before January 1. That would end the case, but leave the Fifth Circuit's precedent in place.
I suppose another state with a similar Article III injury could intervene. I am not certain about the timing as there is a final judgment in place--although a judgment is not really final until a cert petition is disposed of.
If this case stays alive past January, the United States will almost certainly file a cert petition. The new Texas Attorney General will not oppose certiorari and may ask for a summary reversal. I suspect the new AG could even argue that since there is no adversity, there is no longer a live Article III case, and the Fifth Circuit decision should be vacated under Musingwear. I am not entirely sure how Munsingwear applies when the Attorney General switches sides, but we may soon find out. Then again, the Supreme Court routinely decides cases in which there is no adversity, so the case might continue.
Indeed, the Supreme Court might also think it prudent to settle this matter. These challenges can arise in other contexts, and the longer this issue festers, the worse it will be. If so, the Court could appoint an amicus to defend the Fifth Circuit's judgment.
At that point, what will happen? Again, all members of the Fifth Circuit agreed that Texas has standing and the enrolled bill rule doesn't bar review. I suppose the Supreme Court could reject those holdings, but that would be rather transparent.
Once you get to the merits, the Court will have to do some work. I've seen some commentators lead of with a discussion of how many laws might be at risk. One of those statutes is the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022. I'll close where I started. The meaning of the Constitution should not change based on the consequences. Either the House had a quorum or it didn't.
Do I have faith that a majority of the Supreme Court will follow that original meaning of the Constitution? No, I don't. Maybe three votes, at the most--which is often how the Fifth Circuit fares. But don't pretend the Supreme Court is making its ruling based on law.
The post The Quorum Clause Case appeared first on Reason Magazine.
